title: Service Lifetimes
description: Learn how Transient, Scoped, and Singleton lifetimes control how long services live and how many instances are created.

blocks.text: When you register a service in the DI container, you also choose its lifetime. The lifetime determines when a new instance is created and how long it is kept. ASP.NET Core supports three lifetimes: Transient, Scoped, and Singleton. Choosing the right one is critical for correctness, performance, and avoiding memory leaks.

A Transient service gets a new instance every time it is requested. A Scoped service gets one instance per HTTP request. A Singleton service gets one instance for the entire lifetime of the application.

blocks.title: Lifetime Mismatches Cause Bugs
blocks.text: If a Singleton depends on a Scoped service, the Singleton captures the Scoped instance from the first request and reuses it forever. This can cause cross-request data leakage. Always match lifetimes carefully.

Transient services are created each time they are requested. They are lightweight and stateless by design. Because a new instance is built for every injection point, you do not need to worry about shared state or thread safety.
Use Transient for lightweight services with no state, such as validators, formatters, or utility classes that perform calculations.

blocks.title: Registering a Transient Service
blocks.content: Each request for INotifier creates a new EmailNotifier.

blocks.text: Scoped services are created once per HTTP request. If two controllers or services request the same scoped service during the same request, they receive the same instance. When the request ends, the instance is disposed if it implements IDisposable.

The most common scoped service is the database context. Entity Framework Core DbContext is registered as scoped because it tracks entity changes during a single request and should not be shared across requests.

blocks.title: Registering a Scoped DbContext

blocks.text: Singleton services are created once when the container first resolves them, and the same instance is reused for every request until the application shuts down. They must be thread-safe because multiple requests can access them simultaneously.
Use Singleton for stateless services, caches, configuration providers, or logging services. Never register a DbContext or any service that holds request-specific state as Singleton.

blocks.title: Registering a Singleton Cache
blocks.content: A cache is a great example of a singleton because it is shared across all requests.

blocks.title: Lifetime Decision Guide
items: Use Transient for lightweight, stateless services that do not hold data between calls.
Use Scoped for services that should be shared within a single request, such as DbContext.
Use Singleton for services that are expensive to create, stateless, or intentionally shared across all requests.
Avoid injecting Scoped services into Singletons, because the Singleton captures a request-specific instance.
Avoid injecting Singletons into Scoped services unless the Singleton is thread-safe and does not store request state.

terms.definition: A service lifetime where a new instance is created every time the service is requested.
A service lifetime where one instance is created per HTTP request and shared within that request.
A service lifetime where one instance is created for the entire application and reused for every request.
The IServiceCollection where services are registered at startup with their lifetimes.
The property of code that behaves correctly when accessed by multiple threads simultaneously, required for Singletons.

blocks.title: Exercise: Choose and Register Service Lifetimes
blocks.description: Analyze a set of services and decide which lifetime each one needs.
steps: Review these services: ILogger, AppDbContext, IEmailSender, ICache, IStringHasher.
Register each service in Program.cs with the appropriate lifetime.
Create a simple controller that injects each service and logs a message.
Run the application and use logging or breakpoints to verify that Scoped services are reused within a single request.
Attempt to inject a Scoped service into a Singleton and observe the runtime exception or warning.
blocks.expectedOutcome: You will understand which services belong in which lifetime and why mixing lifetimes carelessly causes errors.

items.text: I can describe the difference between Transient, Scoped, and Singleton.
items.hint: New per request, new per injection, one per app.

items.text: I know which lifetime to use for DbContext.
items.hint: Scoped, because it tracks changes within a single request.

items.text: I understand the risk of injecting a Scoped service into a Singleton.
items.hint: The Singleton captures a request-specific instance and reuses it across requests.

items.text: I can explain why Singleton services must be thread-safe.
items.hint: Multiple requests can access the same instance concurrently.

blocks.title: Summary
points: Transient creates a new instance on every request.
Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request.
Singleton creates one instance for the entire application.
Singleton services must be thread-safe because they are shared across requests.
blocks.takeaway: Service lifetimes control object creation and sharing in ASP.NET Core. Choosing the right lifetime prevents bugs, memory leaks, and hard-to-reproduce race conditions.
